summary.text: Prefix masses evolve by a rounded averaging recurrence; reversing and complementing this recurrence turns stabilization into the first time a floor-averaging profile \(D_{N,t}\) becomes positive at the origin. Spatial monotonicity and comparison of the profiles for \(N\) and \(N+1\) give \(T_N+1\le T_{N+1}\le T_N+2\): one comparison prevents positivity from arriving earlier, while another propagates existing positivity within two averaging steps.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 h_C(m)=\left\lceil\frac m2\right\rceil=\left\lfloor\frac{m+1}{2}\right\rfloor,
 \qquad
 h_F(m)=\left\lfloor\frac m2\right\rfloor.
\]
Thus \(h_C(m)+h_F(m)=m\).

For a finite configuration \(x=(x_0,x_1,\ldots)\), extend it by zeros to the right. One cellular-automaton step produces the masses
\[
 x'_0=h_C(x_0),
 \qquad
 x'_{j+1}=h_C(x_{j+1})+h_F(x_j)\quad(j\geq 0).
\]
Deleting trailing zeros does not change this zero-extended sequence of masses.

For \(j\geq 0\), define the prefix mass
\[
 P_j(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{j-1}x_i,
\]
with \(P_0(x)=0\). From the update rule and the identity
\(h_C(m)+h_F(m)=m\), we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
 P_{j+1}(x')
 &=P_j(x)+h_C(x_j)\\
 &=P_j(x)+\left\lfloor\frac{x_j+1}{2}\right\rfloor\\
 &=\left\lfloor\frac{P_j(x)+P_{j+1}(x)+1}{2}\right\rfloor.
\end{aligned}                                                    \tag{1}
\]
The last equality uses \(x_j=P_{j+1}(x)-P_j(x)\). It can also be checked separately according as \(x_j\) is even or odd.

Fix an initial mass \(N\), and let \(S_N(t)\) be the configuration after \(t\) steps, beginning with the one-cell configuration \([N]\). Define numbers \(C_N(t,j)\) by
\[
 C_N(0,j)=
 \begin{cases}
 0,&j=0,\\
 N,&j>0,
 \end{cases}                                                     \tag{2}
\]
and
\[
 C_N(t+1,0)=0,
 \qquad
 C_N(t+1,j+1)=
 \left\lfloor\frac{C_N(t,j)+C_N(t,j+1)+1}{2}\right\rfloor.       \tag{3}
\]
The initial values (2) are exactly the prefix masses of \([N]\), and (3) is (1). Induction on \(t\) therefore gives
\[
 P_j(S_N(t))=C_N(t,j)                                             \tag{4}
\]
for every \(t,j\geq0\).

We now introduce the auxiliary defect process that contains the main argument. For \(N,t,k\geq0\), let
\[
 D_N(0,k)=
 \begin{cases}
 0,&k+1<N,\\
 k+1,&N\leq k+1,
 \end{cases}                                                     \tag{5}
\]
and
\[
 D_N(t+1,k)=
 \left\lfloor\frac{D_N(t,k)+D_N(t,k+1)}2\right\rfloor.           \tag{6}
\]
We establish several elementary properties of this process.

First, for all \(N,t,k\),
\[
 D_N(t,k)\leq k+1.                                                \tag{7}
\]
At time zero this follows immediately from (5). If it holds at time \(t\), then
\[
 D_N(t+1,k)
 \leq \left\lfloor\frac{(k+1)+(k+2)}2\right\rfloor=k+1,
\]
which proves (7) by induction.

Moreover, in the right-hand tail one has the exact formula
\[
 N\leq k+1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad D_N(t,k)=k+1.                \tag{8}
\]
Indeed, this is true initially by (5). If it holds at positions \(k\) and \(k+1\), then (6) gives
\[
 D_N(t+1,k)=\left\lfloor\frac{(k+1)+(k+2)}2\right\rfloor=k+1.
\]

The \(C\)- and \(D\)-processes are related by reflection. For \(j<N\),
\[
 C_N(t,j)=N-D_N(t,N-1-j).                                        \tag{9}
\]
Here and below all quantities are nonnegative integers. To prove (9), use induction on \(t\). At \(t=0\), if \(j=0\), the relevant defect is \(D_N(0,N-1)=N\), so both sides are zero. If \(0<j<N\), then
\(N-1-j+1=N-j<N\), so the relevant initial defect is zero, and both sides equal \(N\).

For the induction step, the case \(j=0\) follows from (8): the reflected defect remains \(N\), while \(C_N(t+1,0)=0\). If \(j>0\), apply the induction hypothesis to the two neighboring prefix values in (3). The only arithmetic identity needed is
\[
 \left\lfloor\frac{(N-a)+(N-b)+1}{2}\right\rfloor
 =N-\left\lfloor\frac{a+b}{2}\right\rfloor                     \tag{10}
\]
whenever \(0\leq a,b\leq N\). This follows by considering the parity of \(a+b\), or directly from the defining inequalities for integer division. The bounds needed to apply (10) follow from (7), since the reflected indices in question are at most \(N-1\). Formula (6) then turns the right side of (10) into the reflected defect at time \(t+1\), proving (9).

We also need the following spatial properties. The process is nondecreasing in \(k\):
\[
 D_N(t,k)\leq D_N(t,k+1).                                        \tag{11}
\]
At time zero, this follows by considering whether each of \(k+1\) and \(k+2\) is below \(N\). If both are below \(N\), both values are zero; if the threshold is crossed, the right value is positive; and if both are at or beyond the threshold, the values are \(k+1\) and \(k+2\). The induction step follows because averaging and taking a floor are monotone in both arguments.

A stronger statement holds after positivity begins:
\[
 D_N(t,k)>0
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 D_N(t,k)+1\leq D_N(t,k+1).                                     \tag{12}
\]
We prove this by induction on \(t\). At time zero, positivity excludes the zero branch of (5), so the two adjacent values are \(k+1\) and \(k+2\).

For the induction step, put
\[
 a=D_N(t,k),\qquad b=D_N(t,k+1),\qquad c=D_N(t,k+2).
\]
Suppose
\[
 D_N(t+1,k)=\left\lfloor\frac{a+b}{2}\right\rfloor>0.           \tag{13}
\]
By (11), \(a\leq b\). There are two cases.

If \(a>0\), the induction hypothesis at \(k\) gives \(b\geq a+1\). Hence \(b>0\), and the induction hypothesis at \(k+1\) gives \(c\geq b+1\). Consequently
\[
 b+c\geq a+b+2,
\]
so
\[
 \left\lfloor\frac{b+c}{2}\right\rfloor
 \geq
 \left\lfloor\frac{a+b}{2}\right\rfloor+1.
\]

If \(a=0\), (13) implies \(b\geq2\). Thus \(b>0\), so the induction hypothesis at \(k+1\) gives \(c\geq b+1\). It follows that
\[
 \left\lfloor\frac{b+c}{2}\right\rfloor
 \geq \left\lfloor\frac{2b+1}{2}\right\rfloor=b
 \geq \left\lfloor\frac b2\right\rfloor+1
 =\left\lfloor\frac{a+b}{2}\right\rfloor+1.
\]
This proves (12) in both cases.

Combining (7) and (12) yields a useful rigidity statement:
\[
 D_N(t,0)>0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad D_N(t,k)=k+1
 \quad\hbox{for every }k\geq0.                                  \tag{14}
\]
Indeed, (7) gives \(D_N(t,0)\leq1\), so positivity forces
\(D_N(t,0)=1\). If \(D_N(t,k)=k+1\), then (12) gives
\(D_N(t,k+1)\geq k+2\), while (7) gives the reverse inequality. Induction on \(k\) proves (14).

For completeness, the \(C\)-process also has the constant right tail
\[
 j\geq N\quad\Longrightarrow\quad C_N(t,j)=N.                   \tag{15}
\]
This follows by induction from (2) and (3). Away from the boundary, both inputs to (3) are \(N\), giving \(N\) again. At the boundary, the left input is bounded above by \(N\) and bounded below by its index, while the right input equals \(N\); these bounds force the rounded average to equal \(N\). Equivalently, those bounds themselves follow inductively from
\[
 j\leq C_N(t,j)\leq N\qquad(j\leq N),
\]
using (3).

We can now characterize stability. Assume \(N\geq1\). We claim
\[
 S_N(t)=[1,1,\ldots,1]\text{ (\(N\) entries)}
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad D_N(t,0)>0.                       \tag{16}
\]

For the forward implication, the prefix mass through the first \(N-1\) cells is \(N-1\). By (4) and (9),
\[
 N-1=C_N(t,N-1)=N-D_N(t,0).
\]
Thus \(D_N(t,0)=1>0\).

Conversely, suppose \(D_N(t,0)>0\). By (14), for \(j<N\),
\[
 D_N(t,N-1-j)=N-j.
\]
Therefore (9) gives
\[
 C_N(t,j)=j\qquad(j<N),
\]
and (15) gives
\[
 C_N(t,j)=N\qquad(j\geq N).
\]
Thus in all cases
\[
 C_N(t,j)=\min(j,N).                                              \tag{17}
\]
Since the mass in cell \(i\) is the difference between consecutive prefix masses, (4) and (17) imply that the zero-extended configuration has mass \(1\) at positions \(0,\ldots,N-1\), and mass \(0\) at all positions \(i\geq N\). Every automaton step deletes all trailing zeros, and the initial positive configuration has no trailing zero. Hence the actual finite list is exactly \(N\) copies of \(1\). This proves (16).

It remains to compare the first positivity times of the defect processes for consecutive values of \(N\). We first prove three comparison inequalities.

The first is the shifted comparison
\[
 D_N(t,k)\leq D_{N+1}(t,k+1).                                   \tag{18}
\]
At time zero, the conditions
\(k+1<N\) and \(k+2<N+1\) are equivalent. Thus either both sides are zero, or the left side is \(k+1\) and the right side is \(k+2\). The induction step follows from (6), monotonicity of floor division, and the induction hypothesis at \(k\) and \(k+1\).

The second comparison moves one step forward in time:
\[
 D_{N+1}(t+1,k)\leq D_N(t,k).                                   \tag{19}
\]
For \(t=0\), first suppose \(k+1<N\). Then both initial values
\(D_{N+1}(0,k)\) and \(D_{N+1}(0,k+1)\) are zero, so the left side is zero. If instead \(N\leq k+1\), the right side is \(k+1\). Each of the two entries averaged on the left is bounded respectively by \(k+1\) and \(k+2\), by (7), and hence their average has floor at most
\[
 \left\lfloor\frac{(k+1)+(k+2)}2\right\rfloor=k+1.
\]
This proves the base case. For the induction step, expand both sides by (6) and apply the induction hypothesis at the two neighboring positions; monotonicity of the rounded average proves (19).

The third comparison is stronger under a positivity assumption:
\[
 D_N(t,k)>0
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 D_N(t,k)+2\leq D_{N+1}(t,k+2).                                 \tag{20}
\]
At time zero, positivity means \(N\leq k+1\). Hence
\[
 D_N(0,k)=k+1,
 \qquad
 D_{N+1}(0,k+2)=k+3,
\]
so equality holds in (20).

For the induction step, write
\[
 a=D_N(t,k),\quad b=D_N(t,k+1),
\]
\[
 y_0=D_{N+1}(t,k+2),\quad y_1=D_{N+1}(t,k+3).
\]
Suppose \(\lfloor(a+b)/2\rfloor>0\). Again split into two cases.

If \(a>0\), then \(b>0\) by (11). The induction hypothesis applied at \(k\) and \(k+1\) gives
\[
 y_0\geq a+2,
 \qquad
 y_1\geq b+2.
\]
Therefore
\[
 \left\lfloor\frac{y_0+y_1}{2}\right\rfloor
 \geq
 \left\lfloor\frac{a+b+4}{2}\right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor\frac{a+b}{2}\right\rfloor+2.
\]

If \(a=0\), positivity of \(\lfloor(a+b)/2\rfloor\) gives \(b\geq2\). Comparison (18), applied at \(k+1\), gives \(y_0\geq b\), while the induction hypothesis applied to the positive value \(b\) gives \(y_1\geq b+2\). Hence
\[
 \left\lfloor\frac{y_0+y_1}{2}\right\rfloor\geq b+1.
\]
Since \(b\geq2\),
\[
 b+1\geq \left\lfloor\frac b2\right\rfloor+2
 =\left\lfloor\frac{a+b}{2}\right\rfloor+2.
\]
Thus (20) holds in the second case as well.

We also note that \(D_N(t,k)\) is nondecreasing in time:
\[
 D_N(t,k)\leq D_N(t+1,k).                                       \tag{21}
\]
Indeed, (11) says \(D_N(t,k+1)\geq D_N(t,k)\), so
\[
 D_N(t+1,k)
 =\left\lfloor\frac{D_N(t,k)+D_N(t,k+1)}2\right\rfloor
 \geq D_N(t,k).
\]

The preceding comparisons imply that positivity for mass \(N\) produces positivity for mass \(N+1\) within two additional steps:
\[
 D_N(t,0)>0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad D_{N+1}(t+2,0)>0.          \tag{22}
\]
Let \(q=D_N(t,0)>0\). By (18) and (20), respectively,
\[
 D_{N+1}(t,1)\geq q,
 \qquad
 D_{N+1}(t,2)\geq q+2.
\]
Since \(q\geq1\), their sum is at least \(4\), and therefore
\[
 D_{N+1}(t+1,1)
 =\left\lfloor
 \frac{D_{N+1}(t,1)+D_{N+1}(t,2)}2
 \right\rfloor\geq2.
\]
The value \(D_{N+1}(t+1,0)\) is nonnegative, so one more averaging step gives
\[
 D_{N+1}(t+2,0)
 =\left\lfloor
 \frac{D_{N+1}(t+1,0)+D_{N+1}(t+1,1)}2
 \right\rfloor\geq1,
\]
which proves (22).

Define the first positivity time
\[
 T(N)=\min\{t\geq0:D_N(t,0)>0\}.                                \tag{23}
\]
This minimum exists. For \(N=0\), the initial value is already positive. Inductively, if positivity occurs for \(N\) at some time \(t\), then (22) gives positivity for \(N+1\) at time \(t+2\). Thus the set in (23) is nonempty for every \(N\).

By (16), for every \(N\geq1\), the times at which the cellular automaton has reached the stable configuration are exactly the times at which \(D_N(t,0)>0\). Consequently
\[
 a(N)=T(N)\qquad(N\geq1).                                       \tag{24}
\]
Notice also from (21) that once positivity occurs, it persists.

We now bound the difference between consecutive first positivity times. Applying (22) with \(t=T(N)\) gives
\[
 T(N+1)\leq T(N)+2.                                              \tag{25}
\]

For the lower bound, assume \(N\geq1\). We prove
\[
 T(N)+1\leq T(N+1).                                              \tag{26}
\]
Suppose contrariwise that \(T(N+1)\leq T(N)\). By positivity at time \(T(N+1)\) and temporal monotonicity (21), this implies
\[
 D_{N+1}(T(N),0)>0.                                              \tag{27}
\]
There are two cases.

If \(T(N)=0\), then \(D_N(0,0)>0\). From (5), this says that \(1<N\) is false, hence \(N\leq1\). Since \(N\geq1\), we have \(N=1\). But then (27) says \(D_2(0,0)>0\), whereas (5) gives \(D_2(0,0)=0\), a contradiction.

If \(T(N)=s+1\), minimality of \(T(N)\) gives
\[
 D_N(s,0)=0.
\]
Comparison (19), with this \(s\) and \(k=0\), yields
\[
 D_{N+1}(s+1,0)\leq D_N(s,0)=0.
\]
Thus \(D_{N+1}(T(N),0)=0\), contradicting (27). This proves (26).

Combining (25) and (26), the integer \(T(N+1)\) lies between
\(T(N)+1\) and \(T(N)+2\), inclusive. Therefore, for every \(N\geq1\),
\[
 T(N+1)=T(N)+1
 \quad\text{or}\quad
 T(N+1)=T(N)+2.
\]
Finally substitute \(a(N)=T(N)\) from (24). We conclude that for every integer \(N\geq1\),
\[
 \boxed{\ a(N+1)-a(N)\in\{1,2\}\ },
\]
or equivalently,
\[
 a(N+1)=a(N)+1\quad\text{or}\quad a(N+1)=a(N)+2.
\]
